story.headline: Iran hits Kuwait and Bahrain after Qeshm strike
story.summary: After US jets struck an IRGC missile site on Qeshm island, Iran fired drones at US targets in Kuwait and Bahrain on 18 November.
story.display_body: Iran fired drones at US military targets in Kuwait and Bahrain on Wednesday 18 November, hours after US jets struck a Revolutionary Guards missile site on Iran's Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait's army said it was intercepting "hostile drones", and Iran's army said its combat and kamikaze drones had targeted US Patriot air-defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms there. Bahrain's armed forces said they had repelled "Iranian air attacks"; the kingdom has now been targeted four times since Friday 13 November, after a lull since September. A US military official, speaking anonymously to AFP, called the Qeshm strike "self-defence" against "aggression targeting US personnel and interests". That is Washington's own description; Tehran says it acted against repeated US drone incursions into its airspace, and neither side's account can be independently checked. The US had already struck Qeshm in early November. Separately, the logistics arm of the Emirati oil company Adnoc said one of its ships was attacked in the strait on Tuesday 17 November, injuring 11 crew; one sailor is missing. Iran's army chief, General Amir Hatami, threatened a "more devastating" response "without geographical limits" if Iranian territory is hit again. Kuwait's foreign ministry called the attack a "flagrant violation" of its sovereignty, and Qatar, which mediates between Washington and Tehran, warned of a "dangerous escalation".
story.why: the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February has been running as intermittent strikes since the April ceasefire broke down over the summer. Iran hitting two Gulf states in one night, after weeks of fighting focused on shipping, widens it again. The escalation comes a day before Donald Trump meets Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, where the Middle East war is expected to be on the agenda.

story.headline: Xi hosts Putin, then greets Trump in Shenzhen
story.summary: Xi and Putin held talks in Shenzhen at APEC on 18 November and Xi greeted Trump at the airport before a three-way meeting on 19 November.
story.display_body: Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held talks in Shenzhen on Wednesday 18 November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, and Xi then greeted Donald Trump in person at Shenzhen airport, ahead of a three-way meeting set for Thursday 19 November. According to the Kremlin's transcript, Xi called it their 50th meeting since 2013 and said the two countries must help "shape a multipolar world". Speaking at the APEC business summit earlier the same day, Putin called Western powers "former hegemons" and said sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions cannot halt competitors' growth. Chinese presidents rarely greet visitors in person on arrival, so meeting Trump at the airport was an unusual gesture. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera expect few concrete outcomes. The US–China talks are clouded by a US criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore data-centre firm suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of US export controls. Nuclear arms control is seen as the one area where all three could find common ground.
story.why: a leaders' meeting of the US, China and Russia without Europe at the table is what Kyiv and European capitals fear could settle questions about Ukraine over their heads. Swiss exports and sanctions policy are tied to both the US and the EU, so any framework that comes out of it affects Switzerland too.

story.headline: Eisenkot ally elected Knesset speaker
story.summary: Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, was elected Knesset speaker with 66 votes on 17 November, replacing Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana.
story.display_body: Israel's new parliament elected Matan Kahana, an ally of opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, as its speaker late on Tuesday 17 November, with 66 of the 120 votes. Kahana, a 54-year-old former fighter pilot and religious-affairs minister in the Bennett–Lapid government, replaces Amir Ohana, a close ally of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who had held the post since 2022. The speaker leads sittings and helps set the parliamentary agenda, which gives Eisenkot's camp control of the timetable before any government is formed. Eisenkot has said he wants to undo Netanyahu's judicial overhaul and set up a commission of inquiry into the security failures before the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023. The vote relied on support from Arab lawmakers. Before it, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the 19 newly elected Arab members "supporters of terror".
story.why: it is the first vote since the 27 October election to show that Eisenkot, whom President Isaac Herzog has asked to form a government, can command a majority in parliament.

story.headline: Peltola flips Alaska Senate seat
story.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola won Alaska's Senate race with 50.12% of first-round votes, unseating Republican Dan Sullivan.
story.display_body: Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's US Senate seat, unseating Republican Dan Sullivan, after a two-week count of the Tuesday 3 November midterm vote. The Alaska Division of Elections' unofficial results, updated on Tuesday 17 November, give Peltola 144,302 votes (50.12%) to Sullivan's 131,844 (45.80%). That puts her just over the majority needed to win in the first round under Alaska's ranked-choice system. A second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. took 4,760 votes. A New York Times report had alleged that Peltola aides tried to use him to draw votes from the senator; Peltola denies knowing of any such plan, and her margin is larger than his total. DW reports that Democrats now hold 56 of the 100 Senate seats, with Alaska the ninth Republican-held seat to flip and the last race to be called. Peltola is the state's first Democratic senator in almost 20 years.
story.why: with the last race called, the Senate is settled, and from January it can block the administration's nominees and legislation.

story.headline: Strasbourg orders Turkey to free MP Atalay
story.summary: The ECHR ruled on 17 November that Turkey must release jailed MP Can Atalay and let him take his seat, finding his detention aimed to silence him.
story.display_body: The European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday 17 November that Turkey must immediately release the jailed lawyer and elected MP Şerafettin Can Atalay and let him take up his seat in parliament. By six votes to one, the Chamber found violations of his right to liberty, his right to free elections, and Article 18, which bars restricting rights for an improper purpose. The court found that his detention "had been intended to silence him". Atalay was sentenced to 18 years in 2022 over the 2013 Gezi Park protests and elected for Hatay in May 2023. Turkey's Constitutional Court twice ruled that he had parliamentary immunity, but the Court of Cassation refused to apply those rulings. The Strasbourg court called that refusal "unprecedented" and contrary to the rule of law. It awarded him €32,500. Under the court's rules, a Chamber judgment is not final for three months, during which either party may ask for a referral to the Grand Chamber.
story.why: Turkey has refused to comply with similar Strasbourg orders in the cases of Osman Kavala and Selahattin Demirtaş. The ruling comes the same week as the takeover of the Sozcu TV channel, and it tests again whether Ankara accepts the Council of Europe court.

story.headline: ADF attacks kill 75 in Ituri
story.summary: Attacks attributed to the ADF killed at least 75 civilians in Mambasa territory, Ituri, over a week ending 14 November.
story.display_body: At least 75 civilians have been killed in a week of attacks attributed to the ADF armed group in Mambasa territory, in the Ituri province of eastern DR Congo, local civil society said, the latest on Saturday 14 November at Ekatu. More than fifteen villages were hit and about forty people abducted, according to civil-society leaders in Mambasa, who say no military response followed their warnings. The ADF (Allied Democratic Forces) is a group of Ugandan origin that has pledged allegiance to the Islamic State. Its fighters operate in small units of about twenty, and survivors have fled towards Beni and Butembo without aid. The toll comes from local groups and has not been confirmed by the army or the UN.

story.headline: Poll: AHV VAT rise and marriage-tax plan trail
story.summary: The second SRG/GFS Bern poll shows the AHV VAT rise at 46% yes, the fireworks initiative at 63% yes, the fairness initiative at 40% yes and the war-material law at 49-46.
story.display_body: Two of the four federal proposals on the Sunday 29 November ballot would go against the Federal Council's and parliament's recommendations if the vote were held now, the second SRG poll by GFS Bern, published on Wednesday 18 November, shows. The VAT increase of 0.4 percentage points to fund the 13th AHV/AVS pension (the state old-age pension) would fail, with 51% against and 46% in favour. Over-65s are the only age group still narrowly in favour (53%). The fireworks initiative would pass with 63% in favour, although that share has dropped. The Centre party's "fairness" initiative on how married couples are taxed (the "marriage penalty") has swung from a lead to 40% yes and 54% no. The revised war-material law, which eases rules on arms exports, is at 49% yes to 46% no, a statistical tie given the ±2.8-point margin of error. The survey ran from 4 to 11 November among 13,527 voters, combining 510 phone interviews with weighted online responses from people who chose to take part. Polls measure opinion, not the outcome, and popular initiatives also need a majority of cantons.
story.why: if the VAT rise fails, the 13th pension, which voters approved in March 2024, still has no funding beyond the AHV fund, which pays it in 2026 and 2027. A rise could take effect in 2028 at the earliest.

story.headline: Bern seeks longer Alpine rail freight aid
story.summary: The Federal Council proposed extending transalpine combined-transport subsidies to 2035, at 486 million francs, as rail's share fell to 68.6%.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 18 November asked parliament to keep subsidising rail freight through the Alps for longer, as the railways' share of that traffic fell for a fourth year running. The share stood at 68.6% in 2025. The government blames poor quality and reliability on the European north–south corridors, especially construction work and closures in Germany, and expects no turnaround before the end of the decade. It proposes extending operating subsidies for unaccompanied combined transport (trailers and containers carried by train, without the lorry cab) from 2030 to 2035. It would also scrap the rule that subsidies per shipment must fall every year, so that the total starts to fall only from 2030. That means about 59 million francs a year from 2027 to 2030 and 486 million francs in total to 2035, paid from the mineral-oil tax. The bill responds to two identical parliamentary motions (26.3004 and 26.3009).
story.why: moving freight from road to rail is a constitutional goal, written in after the 1994 Alpine Initiative. A falling rail share means more lorries on the Gotthard and San Bernardino roads, and the extra subsidy is the government admitting the problem lies largely with German infrastructure, which Switzerland does not control.

story.headline: EU health deal key to Swiss medicine supply
story.summary: A Federal Council report says the Bilaterals III health agreement would give Switzerland full access to EU health-security mechanisms for medicine supply.
story.display_body: The Federal Council said on Wednesday 18 November that the health agreement in the Bilaterals III package with the EU would give Switzerland its main legal basis for working with the EU on securing medicine supplies. It adopted a report, requested by National Councillor Golay's postulate 24.3216, which notes that shortages of medicines are rising in Switzerland. As a non-member, Switzerland today uses only those EU initiatives that are open to third countries and need no specific legal basis. It has no access, or only very limited access, to the EU's central crisis mechanisms. The report says the health agreement would give Switzerland full access to the EU's health-security mechanisms.

story.headline: Signature-forgery suspicions fall sharply
story.summary: The Federal Council said suspected forgeries in signature collections fell to a very low level after 2024 measures and no new law is needed.
story.display_body: Suspected forgeries in signature collections for popular initiatives and referendums have fallen to "a very low level" since 2024, and no new law is needed for now, the Federal Council said in a report on Wednesday 18 November. The Federal Chancellery tightened checks after the scale of suspected forgeries came to light in September 2024. It also set up online reporting of suspicious signatures with the cantons and communes. It is examining how AI could help it check signatures. Since 2022 it has filed five criminal complaints for suspected electoral fraud with the Office of the Attorney General.

story.headline: Self-correcting qubits pass break-even twice
story.summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) spreads one "logical" qubit across many physical degrees of freedom so that errors can be spotted and undone.
story.display_body: Quantum error correction (QEC) spreads one "logical" qubit across many physical degrees of freedom so that errors can be spotted and undone. The usual way is active: measure an error signature, then have classical electronics apply a fix, which is slow and needs high-fidelity readout. Autonomous QEC instead builds the fix into the hardware, using engineered drives and dissipation (deliberately leaking the error's entropy into a helper qubit that is then reset), with no measurement or feedback loop at all. The benchmark is "break-even": a logical qubit that lives longer than the best physical qubit in the same device. Both groups store the qubit as photons in a superconducting microwave cavity and protect it against photon loss, the dominant error. The Shenzhen team's protected qubit lives about 2.0 ms, 18% longer than its best physical qubit, and they use it as a sensor to gain 6.3 dB in precision on a small frequency shift. The Tsinghua team uses a general recipe derived from quantum channel simulation that can in principle implement any recovery operation, and reaches 1.04 times break-even. Both margins are small, and active QEC on bosonic codes has already gone further beyond break-even.
story.why: crossing break-even without measurement shows that error correction can, in part, be wired into the physics of the device rather than run by fast classical control, which could ease one of the hardest scaling problems in quantum computers.

story.headline: Neutrinos take the Sun's core temperature
story.summary: Neutrinos from the Sun's core escape straight through it, so they are the only direct messenger from where fusion happens.
story.display_body: Neutrinos from the Sun's core escape straight through it, so they are the only direct messenger from where fusion happens. Boron-8 neutrinos are a useful probe because the rate at which they are made is very sensitive to core temperature, and the way they change "flavour" on the way out depends on the electron density they cross. Using 5,805 days of data from the Super-Kamiokande water detector in Japan (phases I to IV), the collaboration works backwards to an outer bound on the size of the fusion core and to its density and temperature. For the standard high-metallicity solar model, the core is bounded at 0.499 solar radii at 90% confidence, tightening to 0.268 solar radii when combined with Canada's SNO experiment. The inferred central temperature is 15.599 million K, with a quoted uncertainty of about 1,600 K. That precision holds only within the assumed solar model; with other models of the Sun's composition, the bounds shift.
story.why: it turns a solar-neutrino detector into a thermometer for the Sun's interior. That is a direct check on the solar models used across astrophysics, including the long-running "solar abundance problem" about how much heavy elements the Sun contains.

story.headline: Zurich catalyst arylates bare C–H bonds
story.summary: Joining two aromatic rings is one of the most common steps in making drugs and materials, and the standard method, cross-coupling, needs both partners to carry pre-installed reactive "handles" such as halogens or boron groups.
story.display_body: Joining two aromatic rings is one of the most common steps in making drugs and materials, and the standard method, cross-coupling, needs both partners to carry pre-installed reactive "handles" such as halogens or boron groups. Direct C–H arylation would skip that step by attaching an aryl group straight onto an ordinary carbon–hydrogen bond, but native molecules offer many similar C–H bonds and little reactivity, so yields and site control have been poor. The University of Zurich team builds a tailored chemical microenvironment around a palladium dicarboxylate catalyst so it picks the least crowded C–H site, and pairs an advanced palladium(II) precatalyst with designed diaryliodonium reagents to deliver the aryl group efficiently. The method works on electron-rich and electron-poor arenes, and even plain benzene, normally a hard case, takes successive aryl groups in a controlled way. Because conditions are mild, it tolerates groups that would react in ordinary cross-coupling, such as iodides, triflates and boronate esters, which makes "late-stage" modification of complex molecules possible.
story.why: removing the pre-functionalisation step can shorten synthetic routes in pharmaceutical chemistry. The work comes from a University of Zurich group.

story.headline: Curved nanocarbon gains an aromatic ring
story.summary: Five-membered carbon rings are what make sheets of graphene-like carbon curve into bowls and balls such as fullerenes, but in those structures the five-membered rings are usually not aromatic (they lack the extra stability of benzene-like e.
story.display_body: Five-membered carbon rings are what make sheets of graphene-like carbon curve into bowls and balls such as fullerenes, but in those structures the five-membered rings are usually not aromatic (they lack the extra stability of benzene-like electron sharing). The team made pentabenzocorannulenide, a bowl-shaped carbon anion whose central ring is a cyclopentadienide, the negatively charged, aromatic five-membered ring familiar from organometallic chemistry. They produce it by cleaving a carbon–carbon bond in a precursor, a step driven by the stability gained on becoming aromatic. X-ray crystallography and quantum chemical calculations show bonding and electronic properties unlike corannulene, fullerenes or nanotube end caps. The molecule's conjugate acid is exceptionally strong, and the bowl can bind a metal atom across its central ring.
story.why: it adds a new building block to curved carbon chemistry, a field that feeds into organic electronics and molecular materials.

story.headline: Later generations age with better memory
story.summary: The chance of developing dementia at any given age has been falling in Europe and the US, by about 13% per decade in pooled estimates, but it has been unclear why.
story.display_body: The chance of developing dementia at any given age has been falling in Europe and the US, by about 13% per decade in pooled estimates, but it has been unclear why. One possibility is that later generations start old age with more cognitive reserve; another is that they decline more slowly. The Oslo-led team analysed about 783,000 episodic-memory tests from about 219,000 people in five long-running studies, some followed for 30 years. They find both: later-born generations enter old age with higher memory scores and lose memory more slowly afterwards, a "double dividend" large enough, they argue, to account for the fall in dementia incidence. The gains are concentrated among people who would otherwise decline fastest, and slower memory decline goes with lower rates of clinical impairment and slower shrinkage of the hippocampus, a memory centre. The authors argue that trends affecting everyone at the same calendar time do not explain the pattern. This is an observational analysis, so it shows associations across birth cohorts rather than which specific changes caused them.
story.why: memory level is built mostly in childhood and early life, while the rate of decline is shaped by adult conditions, so the authors conclude that keeping dementia rates falling needs brain-health policy across the whole lifespan, not only interventions in old age.

story.headline: Neanderthal variant reshapes the visual lobe
story.summary: Neanderthal skulls were longer and less rounded than ours, hinting at different proportions of brain regions, and most people outside Africa carry a few percent of Neanderthal DNA from interbreeding.
story.display_body: Neanderthal skulls were longer and less rounded than ours, hinting at different proportions of brain regions, and most people outside Africa carry a few percent of Neanderthal DNA from interbreeding. Hugo Zeberg and Nobel laureate Svante Pääbo report that a common genetic variant affecting the size of the occipital lobe, the brain region at the back that processes vision, was inherited from Neanderthals. It sits in predicted transcription-factor binding sites near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, and carriers show altered DAAM1 activity. Each copy of the variant goes with an occipital lobe about 0.85 cm³ smaller. People with two copies have almost 10% lower schizophrenia risk, an association not seen for Neanderthal ancestry as a whole. Any link to cognition or schooling is small or absent, at most about two weeks of education per copy against an average of about 15 years. These are genetic associations in present-day people; the paper does not show the mechanism linking lobe size and schizophrenia risk.
story.why: it is one of the clearest cases of a single archaic variant visibly changing human brain anatomy today, and it cuts against the idea that Neanderthal-derived brain variants must have cognitive costs.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology
Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology

story.headline: Brain's blood barrier imports protective proteins
story.summary: The blood–brain barrier, the lining of the brain's blood vessels, is usually described by what it keeps out, and Alzheimer's research has focused on how it becomes leaky late in disease.
story.display_body: The blood–brain barrier, the lining of the brain's blood vessels, is usually described by what it keeps out, and Alzheimer's research has focused on how it becomes leaky late in disease. Andrew Yang's group at the Gladstone Institutes labelled the full set of blood proteins in mice, put them back into the bloodstream, and tracked which ones ended up in brain tissue. Of 861 proteins tracked, 92 crossed, most of them made in distant organs, especially the liver. One, apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1), is carried in through receptors on the barrier and on astrocytes (support cells), where it triggers cholesterol release that helps maintain synapses, the connections between neurons. In a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, the barrier stopped importing APOA1 and similar proteins before it started to leak, alongside loss of synapses and behavioural changes. Mice engineered to make extra APOA1 in the liver showed fewer disease markers. All of this is in mice. The Cell full text was not reachable here, so details come from the institute's release and Nature's news report.
story.why: if Alzheimer's begins partly as a supply failure from the body to the brain, therapies could aim to restore that import rather than only clear amyloid. That idea now needs testing in humans.

story.headline: Gamma-stimulation headset fails Alzheimer's trial
story.summary: Spectris AD is a headset of goggles and headphones that flickers light and clicks at 40 Hz for an hour a day, meant to induce "gamma" brain rhythms.
story.display_body: Spectris AD is a headset of goggles and headphones that flickers light and clicks at 40 Hz for an hour a day, meant to induce "gamma" brain rhythms. Mouse studies suggested this could reduce Alzheimer's pathology. In the HOPE trial, 673 people with Alzheimer's disease used an active or a sham device for 12 months. On the 156-point combined scale of cognition and daily function, the active group declined by 8.97 points and the sham group by 8.82, so there was no benefit on the primary measure. Cognito's release is headlined as showing "consistent slowing" of decline in early symptomatic disease, and its chief executive points to a mild-impairment subgroup and says the company will seek US approval next year. An independent neurologist quoted by Nature calls the trial negative, and post-hoc subgroup findings are hypotheses, not evidence. The full data have not been published in a journal.
story.why: it is the largest test yet of gamma stimulation, and on its primary endpoint the result was null. Any regulatory filing would rest on a subgroup analysis, and readers should weigh the company's framing against that.

story.headline: Phone data trace Ebola outbreak's early spread
story.summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus, one of the Ebola-causing viruses, on 15 May 2026 in Ituri province.
story.display_body: The Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus, one of the Ebola-causing viruses, on 15 May 2026 in Ituri province. Nature reports it has since passed 10,000 confirmed infections and 5,198 deaths, making it the largest Bundibugyo outbreak recorded, with no licensed vaccine or treatment for this species. This Congolese-led team paired detailed case and testing records with anonymised mobile-phone mobility data. Between 10 May and 1 June, the number of health zones reporting cases rose by 12 and of smaller health areas by 49, and human travel out of the first hotspots predicted where infections appeared. Early case numbers doubled roughly every 10 days. The index case had symptoms by 25 April, weeks before detection, and risk rose again 150–200 km away as people travelled along established routes to larger towns.
story.why: it quantifies how weeks of missed detection let the virus travel, and it shows mobility data could guide where to put testing and vaccination when the next outbreak starts.

story.headline: Atlas maps 25 million basal ganglia cells
story.summary: The basal ganglia are deep-brain structures involved in movement, mood and decision-making, and they are implicated in Parkinson's and Huntington's disease, addiction and schizophrenia.
story.display_body: The basal ganglia are deep-brain structures involved in movement, mood and decision-making, and they are implicated in Parkinson's and Huntington's disease, addiction and schizophrenia. The NIH-funded BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network released a package of 26 papers across Cell Press journals mapping 25.5 million cells: 21 million from six human brains, about 3 million from macaques and 1.5 million from marmosets. The data combine gene expression, chemical DNA marks, electrical recordings and DNA folding with each cell's location. Across primates the teams identify 61 cell types conserved over about 76 million years. One study of 1.1 million cells from the striatum, which has no clear anatomical borders, finds six molecularly distinct zones, whose differences blur with age, especially in regions affected by Huntington's disease. The paper texts were not reachable here, so details rest on Nature's report.
story.why: it is a reference map for locating which cell types go wrong in these brain diseases, and a scaffold the project intends to extend to the rest of the brain.

story.headline: Poxvirus core has a gated pore
story.summary: Poxviruses, the family that includes smallpox and mpox, are unusual in copying their genes inside a protein shell, the viral core, after entering a cell.
story.display_body: Poxviruses, the family that includes smallpox and mpox, are unusual in copying their genes inside a protein shell, the viral core, after entering a cell. That means molecules must pass in and out of the core, but how was unclear. Using cryo-electron tomography (3D imaging of frozen samples) on vaccinia virus, the team resolved a portal complex in the core wall at 6.7 Å and its central pore at 4.4 Å. Three viral proteins, E8, E6 and L3, form the pore, which narrows to a positively charged constriction lined by conserved lysines from L3. Mutating those residues impaired viral gene expression and growth.
story.why: a conserved, essential channel in the poxvirus core is a possible drug target against a virus family that includes mpox.
affiliations: Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention

story.headline: Independent method confirms M87* black hole ring
story.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope's 2019 image of the black hole M87, a bright ring around a dark "shadow", was built from very sparse data from a planet-wide array of radio dishes, and turning such data into a picture involves choices.
story.display_body: The Event Horizon Telescope's 2019 image of the black hole M87, a bright ring around a dark "shadow", was built from very sparse data from a planet-wide array of radio dishes, and turning such data into a picture involves choices. Different analyses produced different fine detail, and some outside groups argued the ring itself might be an artefact of the imaging method. This Australian team developed an independent algorithm that uses no assumptions about the source's shape and relies on "closure" quantities, combinations of measurements from three or more telescopes in which each dish's calibration errors cancel. Applied to the original M87 data, it recovers a ring 42.2 ± 1.5 microarcseconds across, which implies a black hole of about 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses viewed about 20° from its jet. This settles the shape question, not the finer structure within the ring.
story.why: it removes the main methodological doubt about one of astronomy's best-known images, using a technique free of the calibration choices the critics challenged.

story.headline: Nearby Type Ia supernova nears its peak
story.summary: The ATLAS survey caught supernova SN 2026ahvu on Monday 2 November 2026 in NGC 1433, a barred spiral galaxy about 50 million light-years away.
story.display_body: The ATLAS survey caught supernova SN 2026ahvu on Monday 2 November 2026 in NGC 1433, a barred spiral galaxy about 50 million light-years away. Keck spectroscopy a day later classified it as a young Type Ia, the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf, and it brightened from magnitude 17 to about 13.5 within days. NOIRLab predicts a peak of magnitude 10.5–12.1 between 18 and 23 November 2026 and is coordinating follow-up with DECam, Gemini and SOAR, inviting other observatories to join. It is one of the nearest Type Ia supernovae since SN 2011fe in 2011, and archival Dark Energy Survey images show the site before the explosion. Because Type Ia supernovae are standard candles for measuring cosmic distances, catching one this early helps test how they ignite. At declination −47°, it never rises above the horizon from Switzerland; observers need to be in the Southern Hemisphere.
story.why: a well-observed nearby Type Ia, followed from before peak, helps calibrate the distance ladder behind measurements of the Universe's expansion rate.

story.headline: Dual quasar sits in overheated gas bubble
story.summary: Galaxy-formation models need quasars, feeding supermassive black holes, to blow hot winds that stop their galaxies forming stars, but that hot, diffuse gas is very hard to see.
story.display_body: Galaxy-formation models need quasars, feeding supermassive black holes, to blow hot winds that stop their galaxies forming stars, but that hot, diffuse gas is very hard to see. One way is the thermal Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect: hot electrons slightly change cosmic-microwave-background light passing through them, leaving a measurable dip at millimetre wavelengths. The team found a pair of quasars at redshift 2.37, seen 2.8 billion years after the Big Bang, inside a hot-gas bubble detected at 6σ. Its thermal energy, 9.7 × 10⁶⁰ erg, is 3.6 times what all the hot gas in the host's dark-matter halo should hold, and at least 0.6% of the quasars' lifetime energy output. There are also hints of hot gas 100–600 kiloparsecs out. It is a single system.
story.why: it is direct calorimetry of quasar feedback, the process models invoke to explain why the most massive galaxies stopped forming stars.
